evidence_quotes.quote: Consequently, when legislation speaks of access, it denotes a specific duty on the part of local government. Such duty includes providing infrastructure for sanitation services as well as the continued servicing of such infrastructure so that it works as intended.

the discussion then evaluates past and present case law to determine the extent to which, and the methods through which, courts are holding local governments accountable for failing to deliver on sanitation services.

its capacity to provide for such services was inhibited by the fact that the applicants were residing on private land, and that in the absence of authority from the private land owner, they had no jurisdiction.

In Section 3, we explore how the legal obligations have found expression in judicial settings through a synopsis of some of the cases in which legal accountability has been pursued and where courts have had the opportunity to adjudicate on local government failures in sanitation services delivery.

Against this combined background, it is now necessary to sketch how the courts have facilitated legal accountability for failure to deliver on sanitation services. Such endeavour is pursued through the lens of four cases: Nokotyana, Beja, Kenton and Msunduzi.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines municipal obligations and failures regarding household and community access to basic sanitation services (e.g., VIP latrines in informal settlements, enclosed vs. unenclosed toilets, sewage reticulation maintenance, and sanitation for farm occupiers) in South Africa.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, it examines constitutional, statutory, and judicial accountability frameworks governing local government sanitation delivery. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it specifically analyses enforcement mechanisms (judicial remedies, structural interdicts, and municipal manager contempt liability) as well as tenure and settlement-status rules directly governing sanitation access (municipal refusals to provide toilets prior to formal township upgrading or on private farm land without landowner consent).
criterion_notes.c3: Published as a legal 'CASE NOTE' based on an LLM thesis, the paper is a pure doctrinal commentary reviewing South African constitutional/statutory provisions and four reported court judgments (Nokotyana, Beja, Kenton, and Mshengu/Msunduzi). It employs no empirical methodology, collects or analyses no primary quantitative or qualitative data, and is not a systematic empirical synthesis; excluded under Exclusion Criterion 1 / code E05.
criterion_notes.c4: While the four discussed court judgments factually involved lack of VIP latrines, unenclosed communal/erf toilets, overflowing sewage pumps, and absence of farm sanitation, the paper itself analyses judicial reasoning and legal remedies (structural interdicts and contempt orders) rather than empirically measuring or reporting household or community sanitation access outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: Because this is a doctrinal case note rather than an empirical study, there is no empirical study design, sampling frame, or measured population-exposure-outcome relationship at the household or community level (unit of discussion is four selected judicial decisions).

study_design: Doctrinal legal commentary / case note (non-empirical analysis of legislation and four judicial decisions)
population_and_sample: Four reported South African court decisions (Nokotyana, Beja, Kenton on Sea Ratepayers Association, and Mshengu/Msunduzi); no empirical household or community sample
exposure: Constitutional and statutory duties of local government to provide basic sanitation (Constitution ss 152, 153, 24, 27; Water Services Act s 3; Municipal Systems Act; Extension of Security of Tenure Act), tenure/settlement-upgrading restrictions, and judicial enforcement remedies (structural interdicts, contempt orders)
outcome: Judicial accountability doctrines and court-ordered legal remedies (e.g., structural interdicts and contempt findings); no empirical household or community sanitation access outcome measured
rationale: Full text matches metadata (Twani & Soyapi 2022, South African Journal on Human Rights). Although the paper addresses sanitation service access (c1) and rule-type legal enforcement and tenure mechanisms governing municipal sanitation obligations (c2), it is a pure doctrinal case note reviewing statutory provisions and four reported court judgments without any primary empirical data, empirical socio-legal fieldwork, quantitative/qualitative empirical analysis, or systematic empirical synthesis (c3 = no). Per Exclusion Criterion 1 ('Pure doctrinal commentary without empirical access evidence'), it is excluded under code E05.
